Done. Output written to `/home/user/gp-rarelink/data/extracted/ssadh/ow-ssadh/per_paper/33393837.json` (valid JSON; all spans checked verbatim against the paper).

**Rows per table:** publications 1; individuals 4; variants 5; phenotypic_features 16; phenotype_checklist 80 (4 × 20 features).

**Individuals:** 4 (three patients described individually in the Results/figures — the most severe, the mildest/normal-IQ one, the Figure 5 8-year-old — plus the previously published Yamakawa et al 2012 boy). Table 2 gives only group counts, so it produced no rows.

**reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant:** `true`.

**Main uncertainties:**
1. Whether the three individually described patients are distinct from the counted cohorts (they are the only people with individual-level detail, so I gave them rows).
2. Zygosity "compound heterozygous" applied to both variants of the most severe patient from one sentence; the second variant got no type.
3. The Yamakawa boy's variant row is `"not reported"` — the link to c.1294A>C is indirect.
4. Marking "normal IQ" as excluding intellectual disability (per D-27).
5. Table 2's group percentages attributed to nobody; no per-patient source column existed, so all `source_reference_in_review` are "not reported" except the Yamakawa row.

I'll start by reading the instructions, schema, and rules files.

1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)
2	
3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The changes from v4 are D-27 and D-29 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the Stage 5 audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10), marked "(v5)". v5 was checked on 20 HA20 papers under D-29 (`poc-ha20-v5-subset`). The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency, the disease caused by germline *ALDH5A1* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ssadh_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *ALDH5A1* variant or a diagnosis of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *ALDH5A1* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *ALDH5A1* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.
157	
158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.
163	
164	## Finish
165	1. Validate that your file parses as JSON.
166	2. Check every span occurs verbatim in the paper.
167	3. Check every row has every schema field.
168	4. Reply with:
169	   - the number of rows per table;
170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

1	Extraction rules (GP-RareLink, v1). These rules apply to every table and every row.
2	
3	1. Use only the supplied document. Do not use outside knowledge about the gene, the disease, specific variants or specific patients. If the document does not state something, the value is "not reported" (for text fields) or null (for numeric and date fields). Never fill a gap from memory.
4	2. Every value must be supported by a verbatim quote copied exactly from the document. Do not paraphrase inside the quote. If no exact quote supports a value, do not emit the value.
5	3. Keep original strings. Record variant descriptions, ages, feature names and labels exactly as printed. Never convert protein-only variant descriptions into cDNA notation, never add a transcript that is not printed, never translate units.
6	4. Three-state phenotypes: a feature is "observed" only when the document says the person has or had it, and "excluded" only when the document explicitly says it was absent, negative or not found in that person. Silence is "not reported". Never turn silence into "excluded".
7	5. One row per real person per document. Relatives described in the document are their own rows with is_proband = false unless the document calls them probands. Do not merge people, and do not create a person the document does not describe.
8	6. Cohort tables: when a table lists many patients, extract each patient row separately with the table's own patient identifier as individual_label_in_paper. Keep the row-to-column alignment of the table; when a cell is empty or marked "-", "NA" or "ND", treat it as not reported.
9	7. Re-reports: if the document says that any of its patients were described in an earlier publication, record that statement and the citation in the publications table. Do not drop the patient.
10	8. Do not infer inheritance or zygosity. "de novo" requires that the document states parental testing showed the variant absent in both parents. "heterozygous" requires that the document says so or the gene is described as monoallelic for that person.
11	9. Prefer "not reported" to a plausible guess. Abstention is correct behaviour.

8	# SSADH Deficiency: Review of the Natural History Study
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	Objective:The SSADHD natural history study was initiated in 2019 to define the natural course and identify biomarkers correlating with severity.Methods:The study is conducted by four institutions: BCH (US clinical), WSU (bioanalytical core), USF (biostatistical core), and Heidelberg (iNTD), with support from the family advocacy group (SSADH Association). Recruitment goals were to study twenty patients on-site at BCH, ten with iNTD, and 25 as a standard-of care-cohort.Results:At this half-way point of this longitudinal study, 28 subjects have been recruited (57% female, mean 9 yrs, range 18 months – 40 years). Epilepsy is present in half and increases in incidence and severity, as do psychiatric symptoms, in adolescence and adulthood. The average Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) was 53 (Verbal score of 56, Non Verbal score of 49), and half scored as having ASD. While there was no correlation between gene variant and phenotypic severity, there were extreme cases of lowest functioning in one individual and highest in another that may have genotype:phenotype correlation. The most common EEG finding was mild background slowing with rare epileptiform activity, whereas high density EEG and MEG showed reduction in the gamma frequency band consistent with GABAergic dysfunction. MR spectroscopy showed elevations in the GABA/NAA ratio in all regions studied with no crossover between subjects and controls.Conclusions:The SSADH Natural History Study is providing a unique opportunity to study the complex pathophysiology longitudinally and derive electrophysiologic, neuroimaging, and laboratory data for correlation and to serve as biomarkers for clinical trials and prognostic assessments in this ultra-rare inherited disorder of GABA metabolism.
13	
14	## Introduction
15	
16	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder of degradation of gamma-amino butyric acid (GABA), the major inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain. GABA is initially metabolized by GABA transaminase, which utilizes pyridoxal-5-phosphate (P5P) as a cofactor and leads to formation of succinic semialdehyde, an unstable and toxic intermediate converted into succinic acid via SSADH (Figure 1). This should lead to entry of succinate into the tricarboxylic acid, leading to the generation of ATP as well as formation of alpha-ketoglutarate which further leads to synthesis of glutamate. There is a 1:1 conversion of glutamate, the major excitatory neurotransmitter of the brain, to GABA, the latter mediated by the enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), which also utilizes P5P as a cofactor. In the absence of SSADH, the succinic semialdehyde is instead converted to gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), also called 4-hydroxybutyric acid, which is detected in physiologic fluids as well as other dicarboxylic acids, including 4,5-dihexanoic acid.
17	
18	The disorder has protean manifestations, with most cases characterized by developmental delay and hypotonia identified within the first two years of life, communication disorder which persists as severe impairment in expressive language, intellectual deficiency, and in many cases a variety of neurological and psychiatric manifestations including epilepsy, ataxia, movement disorders, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, anxiety, sleep disruptions, and hallucinations (Pearl et al 2003a; Pearl et al 2003b; Gibson et al 2003). While the course is typically nonprogressive, there are acute presentations, including infantile encephalopathies (Zeiger et al 2016), as well as evidence of deterioration, especially in adulthood (LaPalme-Remis et al 2015).
19	
20	The disease was first discovered following reports of elevations in GHB (Jakobs et al 1981), leading to confirmation of the enzymatic deficiency (Gibson et al 1983). Mammalian SSADH was purified in 1992 (Chambliss and Gibson 1992), and the ALDH5A1 gene was cloned in 1995 (Chambliss et al 1995) (Figure 2). While the clinical phenotype was then being described (Gibson et al 1983; Pearl et al 2003a; 2003b), a series of experiments emanated from development of a murine model utilizing genetic degradation technology (Hogema et al 2001). The affected micemanifest failure-to-thrive and evolution of absence to vibrissal twitching seizures with lethality by three weeks of age. Preclinical therapeutic trials included taurine (a high constituent of murine breast milk and utilized due to advent of seizures upon weaning of the suckling mice), the GABA-transaminase inhibitor vigabatrin, GHB receptor antagonist NCH-382, GABA(B) receptor antagonist CGP35348 and later named SGS742 (Gupta et al 2002), and the ketogenic diet (Nylen et al 2008) although with concern regarding applicability to patients (Knerr and Pearl 2008). These early studies led to later clinical trials (Pearl et al 2009a; Pearl et al 2014; Schreiber et al 2016) (Figure 3). In addition, investigations elucidated widespread neurometabolic alterations (Gibson et al 2002) and the molecular underpinnings of the disorder, from disease-associated gene variants (Akaboshi et al 2003) to the crystal structure of the enzyme (Kim et al 2009). Subsequent animal studies showed dysfunction of the mTOR pathway with potential rescue using rapalogue therapy (Vogel et al 2015) and early work showing feasibility and promise of enzyme replacement therapy (Vogel et al 2018). Meanwhile, neurophysiologic studies and immunohistochemistry disclosed abnormalities of both GABA (A) and (B) receptor function in the murine model (Wu et al 2006; Buzzi et al 2006), followed by evidence for chronic overuse downregulation of these receptors in patients based on flumazenil-ligand PET (Pearl et al 2009b) and TMS studies focused on GABA’ergic innervation (Reis et al 2012).
21	
22	The SSADH deficiency (SSADHD) natural history study is an NICHD (NIH) sponsored study with a single US site for clinical activity (Boston Children’s Hospital), biorepository and bioanalytical core (Washington State University), and statistical core (Florida State University). There is international recruitment through the iNTD (international Neurotransmitter Disease Association) and involvement by the family advocacy organization, the SADH Association. Patients are evaluated on alternate years on site, and receive annual laboratory testing. Patients unable to attend one of the clinical centers are enrolled into a “standard of care” cohort, with questionnaire based evaluations and procurement of laboratory samples (Figure 4).
23	
24	As an observational study, the objectives upon inception were to justify the incorporation of SSADHD in newborn screening panels by defining the clinical, neurophysiological, and biochemical spectrum and natural course of the disease. Secondary objectives were to identify biomarkers that correlate and predict the clinical presentation and severity, develop a blood spot-based GABA assay adaptable to high-throughput newborn screening platforms, and establish an SSADHD international registry and biobank for future investigations of pathogenesis and therapy. The primary outcomes are a clinical severity score, neuropsychological results, neurophysiological data from transcranial magnetic stimulation, electroencephalography (EEG), and in selected cases high-density EEG and magnetoencephalography (MEG). In addition, MRI and MR spectroscopy with sequences and quantification dedicated to quantification of GABA are administered. The primary goals of the study are to define age-dependent and inter-individual variation of study outcomes and to correlate neurophysiological and biochemical outcomes with clinical outcomes. A secondary goal is to determine the power of neurophysiological and biochemical outcomes measured at baseline to predict clinical outcomes at the end of the study.
25	
26	## Methods
27	
28	The design of the study is prospective, mixed with longitudinal and cross-sectional assessments over a period of five years. The enrollment target was 55 patients total: 20 at BCH, 10 at iNTD, and 25 who were unable to receive on-site diagnostic testing but are included as a standard-of-care cohort for whom historical and laboratory data could be obtained. The BCH patients are recruited from an ongoing registry that includes 143 patients (52% female) as of February 2020, with a median age of 9 years (range 8 weeks – 63 years). Eligible patients are any individual with confirmed SSADH deficiency, via persistent 4-OH-butyric aciduria and pathological ALDH5A1 variants, of any age. Patients in all cohorts receive electronic surveys every six months.
29	
30	The BCH cohort receives comprehensive evaluation every two years, including brain imaging (MRI, MRS), EEG, TMS, and clinical and neuropsychological testing in addition to laboratory specimens including blood, urine, hair, saliva, and stool samples, and in some cases skin biopsy. The laboratory specimens are entered into the biorepository, and measurements include blood GABA, GHB, glutamate, and allopregnanolone in addition to blood spots for GABA. Ancillary measurements and procedures include blood oxidative stress markers (glutathione [GSH], 4-hydroxynonenal [4-HNE], 4-hydroxynonenal glutathione [4-HNE-GSH]), metabolites (D-2-hydroxyglutarate [D-2-HG], succinic semialdehyde [SSA], 4,5-dihydroxyhexanoic acid [DHHA], homocarnosine, urine metabolites (GHB, D-2-HG, SSA), hair GABA and GHB, stool GABA and microbiota, and gene expression with samples banked for RNA-Seq next generation sequencing. In addition, a subset of patients was able to receive high density EEG and MEG testing at BCH for spontaneous recordings as well as evoked somatosensory potentials.
31	
32	Neuropsychological assessments include a clinical parent/subject interview and observations of current behaviors, age-appropriate cognitive and adaptive measures (Mullen Scales of Early Learning; Differential Abilities Scale, Second Edition; Wechsler Abbreviated Scales of Intelligence; Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, 2nd Edition), as well as academic and language measures (Receptive Language and Expressive Language, REEL-3), behavioral measures (Achenbach Adult Behavior Checklist and Child Behavior Checklist), autism spectrum disorders and related symptom measures (Autism Diagnostic Observation Scale; Behavior and Sensory Interests Questionnaire), and motor capabilities using the Movement Assessment Battery for Children – 2nd Edition or MABC-II.
33	
34	Based on the constellation of neurological and psychological impairments in this patient population, an overall Clinical Severity Score was developed to be employed and tested for reliability. This is based on a composite score ranging from 5 (profound impairment) to 25 (no impairment), calculated using scores from five clinically significant subdomains (cognition, communication, motor skills, psychiatric presentation, and epilepsy) (Table 1).
35	
36	Given the recognized variable clinical presentation depending on age, the analysis of clinical characteristics was stratified as above and below 12 years of age. The standard of care cohort was excluded from the analysis due to the nature of the limited visit conducted off-site. Qualitative variables are expressed in percentages and relationship contrasts were analyzed using the chi-square (or Fisher Exact test). Statistical analyses were conducted with SPSS, version 24 (IBM Corp. Released 2016. IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows Version 24.0 Armonk, NY: IBM Corp).
37	
38	## Results
39	
40	At of the time of the July 2020 Conference, 28 SSADH deficiency patients have been recruited into the natural history study, 12 males (43%) and 16 females (57%), with a median age of 9 years and age range of 18 months – 40 years. Controls have been recruited for comparison to our neuroimaging and neurophysiologic procedures, specifically 13 (6 males/46%, 7 females/54%, median age 16 years with age range 6 – 35 years). The BCH on-site cohort is currently composed of 25 subjects, 16 in the pediatric group (< 12 years) and 9 in the adolescent/adult group (12+ years). Their clinical characteristics are shown in Table 2. The SOC cohort has three subjects, two in the pediatric group (< 12 years) and 1 in the adolescent/adult group (12+ years). Epilepsy is a co-morbid diagnosis in half of the patients and increases in incidence during adolescence and adulthood (p = <0.001). The clinical severity of epilepsy also correlated with age based on seizure frequency, showing a stronger association in the older cohort (p = 0.002). There was also an increased incidence of obsessive-compulsive disorder in the older cohort (p = 0.003) as well as severity in psychiatric impairment based on the criteria used in the Clinical Severity Scale (p = 0.09).
41	
42	Of 25 subjects studied with EEG, 16 (64%) had diffuse background slowing (mild in all cases), and only occasional epileptiform features manifest as generalized spike-and-wave in only one (Figure 5), focal spikes in two subjects (ages 5 and 9, and without history of seizures), and sharp waves in two.
43	
44	Neuropsychological evaluations have been completed on 21 subjects. The average full scale IQ measurement was 53 [IQR 49-61, range 30 (floor value) to 87], including verbal of 56 [IQR 46-65, range 30 (floor value) to 95] and non-verbal 49 [IQR 47-62, range 30 (floor value) to 84]. Of 20 patients evaluated with autism scales (ADOS/AOSI), 10 (50%) scored as having autism spectrum disorder. On a test of movement ability, 20/21 (95%) scored < 1^st %-tile and 1/21 (5%) > 1^st %-tile. The median Clinical Severity Scale score for the 28 total subjects was 15 (IQR 12.75-17.25).
45	
46	While there was a correlation between age and epilepsy and psychiatric dysfunction, there was no overall correlation between gene variant and phenotypic severity, although two notable cases were observed at the extremes of severity. A single patient had the maximum severity level (5 of 25), who presented with neonatal hypotonia, infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia on EEG, status epilepticus at age 14 months, neurologic regression, and daily seizures on three antiseizure medicines. The genotype was compound heterozygous c.1294A>C (p.Met432Leu); c.610-2A>G.
47	
48	A single patient had a normal IQ measurement and also had the least severity on the global scale (20 of 25). The genotype was a novel variant c.1321G>A (p.Gly441Arg) and a known variant present in over 5% of the patients: c.612G>A (p.Trp204Ter). This patient had a clinical presentation at 16 months, expressive language deficit, and hypotonia with no seizures and only mild slowing on EEG without epileptiform features.
49	
50	Additional neurophysiologic testing was done in a subset of subjects using somatosensory evoked responses during both high density EEG (64 channels) and MEG, showing suppression of both the gamma and beta activity bands from tactile stimulation of both upper and lower extremities of patients compared to controls (Figure 6).
51	
52	Structural neuroimaging demonstrated T2 hyperintensity in the globus pallidi and dentate nuclei, with additional quantification of these and other signal abnormalities and volumetry as discussed in a separate manuscript in this issue. MR spectroscopy measured GABA in voxels corresponding to the posterior cingulate gyrus, basal ganglia, and occipital cortex with consistent elevation in the GABA/NAA ratio in all subjects, having no overlap with controls.
53	
54	## DISCUSSION
55	
56	SSADH deficiency has protean manifestations, both clinically and metabolically, and prior investigations have led to landmark discoveries including development of a genetically modified murine model, identification of pathogenic ALDH5A1 gene variants, and determination of GABA (A) and (B) receptor dysfunction in humans confirming animal findings. Preclinical and clinical trials have not led to definite therapy for this complex pathophysiology involving alterations in multiple neurotransmitter systems as well as evidence for disrupted autophagy and oxidative metabolism. In order to study the natural history of the disorder and develop biomarkers to better understand its pathophysiology, prognostic determinants, and potential for newborn screening, a natural history study was undertaken by an international collaborative group based at four institutions: BCH as the primary clinical site, WSU as the biorepository core, FSU for statistical core, and the iNTD for international patients, with support and outreach from the SSADH Association, the US family advocacy group. Patients were recruited from a registry maintained at BCH and with help from the SSADH Association for the BCH on-site comprehensive evaluations, as well as standard-of-care patients unable to travel to this site. The iNTD participating sites, based at the Children’s Hospital Heidelberg, is about to initiate recruitment.
57	
58	At this half-way point into the natural history study and at the time of this International SSADH Deficiency conference, recruitment goals have been exceeded at BCH with 25 active subjects, along with recruitment of controls, addition of more sophisticated neurophysiologic studies (high density EEG and MEG) in a subset of patients, and enrollees into the standard-of-care cohort. The group’s clinical characteristics are similar to what has been reported from our registry (DiBacco et al 2018). There is a significant relationship between the presence of epilepsy and its severity, and obsessive-compulsive behaviors and psychiatric dysfunction, in the adolescent and adult cohorts compared to the pediatric one (< 12 years of age). While there was no overall correlation between gene variant and severity, there were notable extremes of phenotypic severity in association with variants that may have prognostic value. That is, the missense variant c.1294A>C (p.Met432Leu) in the most severely affected patient was also published in a 23-month old boy with severe neurological deficits and a nearly identical progressive course to our patient (Yamakawa et al 2012). We are unaware of other cases with this variant. In addition, we had a single patient with a normal fullscale IQ (87) who concomitantly had the highest functioning on the other measures, including the Movement Assessment Battery and Clinical Severity Score who had a novel missense variant (c.1321G>A, p.Gly441Arg) that we suspect correlates with a milder phenotype.
59	
60	The SSADHD Natural History Study has provided us with a unique, unprecedented opportunity to study this complex, ultrarare neurometabolic disorder of GABA degradation longitudinally and to collect a biorepository for a wide range of studies as well as correlation with our neurophysiologic and neuroimaging studies. Use of high density EEG and MEG derived spontaneous and evoked activity demonstrate a decrease in the gamma frequency band in SSADH subjects compared to healthy controls, consistent with impaired GABA-ergic activity and presenting another biomarker that can be used to study neurophysiologic dysfunction. We propose additional studies on this population, including addition of polysomnography and new imaging sequences that allow for metabolic profiling, to further elucidate the complex mechanisms and potential for intervention in this disorder.

Excluded (group counts only): the two subjects with focal spikes (ages 5 and 9), two with sharp waves,
16/25 with background slowing, the other cohort members (28 recruited; registry 143; target 55).
No ' / ' stacked cells in this paper.
"}

  "method_note": "Study-level cohort paper on succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency with no per-patient table: Table 1 is the Clinical Severity Score key (no patients) and Table 2 gives only group counts (N = 16 pediatric and N = 9 adolescent/adult BCH subjects, with percentages), so no rows were created from Table 2. Every value was copied by hand from the Markdown; no script transcribed any table. Only four people are described with individual-level detail and get rows: the 8 year old patient of Figure 5, the 'single patient' with maximum severity, the 'single patient' with normal IQ/least severity, and the 23-month old boy of Yamakawa et al 2012, who is in scope as a previously published person because the paper gives sex, age, variant and features for him. Variant fields are filled only from each person's own sentence; the abstract-level statements ('Epilepsy is present in half', 'half scored as having ASD') and the group percentages in Table 2 were not attributed to anyone. The paper gives no parental testing for any variant, so all inheritance values are 'not reported'. messages.content: 46	While there was a correlation between age and epilepsy and psychiatric dysfunction, there was no overall correlation between gene variant and phenotypic severity, although two notable cases were observed at the extremes of severity. A single patient had the maximum severity level (5 of 25), who presented with neonatal hypotonia, infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia on EEG, status epilepticus at age 14 months, neurologic regression, and daily seizures on three antiseizure medicines. The genotype was compound heterozygous c.1294A>C (p.Met432Leu); c.610-2A>G.

48	A single patient had a normal IQ measurement and also had the least severity on the global scale (20 of 25). The genotype was a novel variant c.1321G>A (p.Gly441Arg) and a known variant present in over 5% of the patients: c.612G>A (p.Trp204Ter). This patient had a clinical presentation at 16 months, expressive language deficit, and hypotonia with no seizures and only mild slowing on EEG without epileptiform features.

58	At this half-way point into the natural history study and at the time of this International SSADH Deficiency conference, recruitment goals have been exceeded at BCH with 25 active subjects, along with recruitment of controls, addition of more sophisticated neurophysiologic studies (high density EEG and MEG) in a subset of patients, and enrollees into the standard-of-care cohort. The group’s clinical characteristics are similar to what has been reported from our registry (DiBacco et al 2018). There is a significant relationship between the presence of epilepsy and its severity, and obsessive-compulsive behaviors and psychiatric dysfunction, in the adolescent and adult cohorts compared to the pediatric one (< 12 years of age). While there was no overall correlation between gene variant and severity, there were notable extremes of phenotypic severity in association with variants that may have prognostic value. That is, the missense variant c.1294A>C (p.Met432Leu) in the most severely affected patient was also published in a 23-month old boy with severe neurological deficits and a nearly identical progressive course to our patient (Yamakawa et al 2012). We are unaware of other cases with this variant. In addition, we had a single patient with a normal fullscale IQ (87) who concomitantly had the highest functioning on the other measures, including the Movement Assessment Battery and Clinical Severity Score who had a novel missense variant (c.1321G>A, p.Gly441Arg) that we suspect correlates with a milder phenotype.

52	Structural neuroimaging demonstrated T2 hyperintensity in the globus pallidi and dentate nuclei, with additional quantification of these and other signal abnormalities and volumetry as discussed in a separate manuscript in this issue. MR spectroscopy measured GABA in voxels corresponding to the posterior cingulate gyrus, basal ganglia, and occipital cortex with consistent elevation in the GABA/NAA ratio in all subjects, having no overlap with controls.

46	While there was a correlation between age and epilepsy and psychiatric dysfunction, there was no overall correlation between gene variant and phenotypic severity, although two notable cases were observed at the extremes of severity. A single patient had the maximum severity level (5 of 25), who presented with neonatal hypotonia, infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia on EEG, status epilepticus at age 14 months, neurologic regression, and daily seizures on three antiseizure medicines. The genotype was compound heterozygous c.1294A>C (p.Met432Leu); c.610-2A>G.
48	A single patient had a normal IQ measurement and also had the least severity on the global scale (20 of 25). The genotype was a novel variant c.1321G>A (p.Gly441Arg) and a known variant present in over 5% of the patients: c.612G>A (p.Trp204Ter). This patient had a clinical presentation at 16 months, expressive language deficit, and hypotonia with no seizures and only mild slowing on EEG without epileptiform features.
58	At this half-way point into the natural history study and at the time of this International SSADH Deficiency conference, recruitment goals have been exceeded at BCH with 25 active subjects, along with recruitment of controls, addition of more sophisticated neurophysiologic studies (high density EEG and MEG) in a subset of patients, and enrollees into the standard-of-care cohort. The group’s clinical characteristics are similar to what has been reported from our registry (DiBacco et al 2018). There is a significant relationship between the presence of epilepsy and its severity, and obsessive-compulsive behaviors and psychiatric dysfunction, in the adolescent and adult cohorts compared to the pediatric one (< 12 years of age). While there was no overall correlation between gene variant and severity, there were notable extremes of phenotypic severity in association with variants that may have prognostic value. That is, the missense variant c.1294A>C (p.Met432Leu) in the most severely affected patient was also published in a 23-month old boy with severe neurological deficits and a nearly identical progressive course to our patient (Yamakawa et al 2012). We are unaware of other cases with this variant. In addition, we had a single patient with a normal fullscale IQ (87) who concomitantly had the highest functioning on the other measures, including the Movement Assessment Battery and Clinical Severity Score who had a novel missense variant (c.1321G>A, p.Gly441Arg) that we suspect correlates with a milder phenotype.

Controls have been recruited for comparison to our neuroimaging and neurophysiologic procedures, specifically 13 (6 males/46%, 7 females/54%, median age 16 years with age range 6 – 35 years). The BCH on-site cohort is currently composed of 25 subjects, 16 in the pediatric group (< 12 years) and 9 in the adolescent/adult group (12+ years). Their clinical characteristics are shown in Table 2. The SOC cohort has three subjects, two in the pediatric group (< 12 years) and 1 in the adolescent/adult group (12+ years). Epilepsy is a co-morbid diagnosis in half of the patients and increases in incidence during adolescence and adulthood (p = <0.001). The clinical severity of epilepsy also correlated with age based on seizure frequency, showing a stronger association in the older cohort (p = 0.002). There was also an increased incidence of obsessive-compulsive disorder in the older cohort (p = 0.003) as well as severity in psychiatric impairment based on the criteria used in the Clinical Severity Scale (p = 0.09).
